subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING APPLICATION TO MENTALLY RETARDED PERSONS

speakeroldname: Mr. William Dean Howe (Hamilton South) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING APPLICATION TO MENTALLY RETARDED PERSONS
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-118, to amend the Juvenile Delinquents Act (application to mentally retarded).

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING APPLICATION TO MENTALLY RETARDED PERSONS
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING APPLICATION TO MENTALLY RETARDED PERSONS
speechtext:
The passage of the Juvenile Delinquents Act marked our recognition that a juvenile charged with an offence against our criminal laws should not, as well for the good of the community as for his own good, be exposed to the usual public and trial process of the criminal courts; and, if adjudged an offender, cannot comprehend and benefit by, and therefore should not undergo, the penal punishment of an adult offender.
Since the passage of the act, scientific technologies enable us to define the mental age of a person in terms of an equivalent chronological age. The purpose of this bill is simply to update the law in accord with these scientific advances and so apply the act to those mentally retarded persons who have a mental age within the age limits protected by the act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.
(Questions answered orally are indicated by an asterisk.)

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE BENEFITS TO CANADIAN WORKERS IN U.S.
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE BENEFITS TO CANADIAN WORKERS IN U.S.
speechtext:
1.	What reasons were given by the representatives of the employment security commissions of Maine and New Hampshire, which prevent an agreement being reached whereby Canadian workers in the United States might be considered eligible for benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act?
2.	In the years 1962 and 1963, how many Canadians were employed on American soil in the states of Maine, New Hampshire, New York and Vermont?
3.	On what basis were agreements reached with the other American states and on what dates were the various agreements signed?
4.	What proposals were submitted by the Canadian government to American authorities with a view to reaching an understanding?

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE BENEFITS TO CANADIAN WORKERS IN U.S.
speechtext:
1. The reasons given by the employment security commission of Maine for being unwilling to enter the reciprocal arrangement were the present condition of their reserve fund, the present economy of the state, and the unevenly balanced flow of workers across the border As almost all the traffic is one way, i.e. persons returning to Canada after working in Maine, the employment security commission thought that there would be too great an increase in the cost to their unemployment insurance fund. The New Hampshire department of employment security stated that New Hampshire was not prepared to make the amendment in its law required to provide for participation in an agreement with Canada.
2.	The national employment service does not have information concerning the number of Canadians that were employed on American soil in the states of Maine, New Hampshire, New York and Vermont.
3.	Agreements with the other American states were reached on the basis that, so far as possible, the provisions of the reciprocal

arrangement already in effect among the states themselves should be extended and applied to Canada provided, however, that it should be optional for each state whether or not to participate in the arrangement with Canada. In the United States each state operates its own unemployment insurance plan. In 1942 the government of Canada and the government of the United States entered into a master agreement in substantially the same terms as that existing among the states. The government of the United States agreed to recommend to each of the states that it carry out the provisions of that agreement with respect to Canada, but no state can be compelled to participate in the agreement if it prefers not to do so. Under this arrangement a person who is working in one of the subscribing states and who subsequently becomes unemployed in Canada may claim benefit from the state in question, through an office of the unemployment insurance commission in Canada. If he is entitled to benefit under the law of that state, the benefit payments are made to him by that state. The local office of the unemployment insurance commission in Canada where he has filed his claim certifies the facts regarding his being unemployed and available for work and forwards such certification to the liable state.
Decision of a state to participate in the agreement is notified by letter to the unemployment insurance commission of Canada either through the bureau of employment security at Washington or directly to the commission. Notices of participation by the states were received as follows: In 1943 from 29 states; between 1943 and 1952 from 14 states; and between 1952 and 1958 from 3 states; leaving four non-participating states, namely Alabama, Iowa, Maine and New Hampshire.
4.	The proposals submitted to the American authorities were that the non-participating states should enter the reciprocal arrangement under the same conditions as the other 46 states which are participating in the arrangement. Such proposals were submitted for consideration on several occasions by letter, by informal discussions between Canadian and American officials, and by discussions at several formal conferences, including meetings in 1959, in 1962 and in 1963.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether he will give a report to the house concerning the situation in Malaysia due to the unprovoked attack on that country by Indonesia; whether the minister will let us know what request has been made by the Malaysian government for assistance from Canada and what response Canada has made to that request; and third, what aid is being given to Malaysia by other commonwealth countries.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Marlin (Secretary of Slate for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the situation in Malaysia has taken a more serious turn within the last few days. The full consequences of the increased intervention by Indonesia are not yet clear. When the prime minister of Malaysia was here the Prime Minister and I conferred with him, with the result that, as the Prime Minister announced on the 29th of July, it was decided that a Canadian military survey group would proceed to Malaysia to determine the kind of assistance which could be provided, bearing in mind particularly the contributions which would be made by other countries. The British government itself is engaged in a similar assessment, and, as my hon. friend knows, the government of Malaysia has recently discussed with the government of the United States what assistance that country might give.
At the present time there is a Malaysian mission in Washington looking over certain possible kinds of purchases, and we anticipate that this group will be in Canada within the course of a very few days. This visit may concern a particular type of aircraft. The decision in that regard will have to be made subject to our own assessment of the situation and the wishes of the government of Malaysia. Consideration will then be given as to the means of financing these operations. The survey group which the Prime Minister announced on July 29 is expected to leave for Malaysia very shortly.

speakeroldname: Righi Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, regard being had to the naked aggression practised by Indonesia against Malaysia, has the government given reconsideration to the question of

terminating once and for all assistance to Indonesia?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the matter is under consideration. I may say that, in consultation with other countries such as Australia, we have considered the matter, but no country has decided to withdraw such assistance to Indonesia, on the theory that assistance of a non-military kind given by western countries has not traditionally borne any political motivation. However, the matter is being reviewed. In the case of Canada, part of our assistance is in respect of aid to students, some of whom are now on their way.

Mr. Speaker, I am not referring to student exchanges; I am referring to food and other such supplies which can have the effect of indirectly rendering available, as the hon. member for Oxford has said, additional foreign exchange, which seems a form of help to Indonesia not justified regardless of the fact that restrictions are not attached to such assistance.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am perfectly aware that the right hon. gentleman was not referring to technical assistance, but I am also aware that other countries have pursued the course I have indicated, and no country has yet cancelled its program. The other form of assistance provided for by Canada in the estimates for 1964-65 is wheat flour in the amount of $350,000. There has been no shipment of flour under this allocation. As I indicated a moment ago, this whole question is under consideration. I would not wish at this time, as external affairs minister, to subscribe summarily to the statement made by the right hon. gentleman a few moments ago.

Mr. Speaker, this is not a question of summarily subscribing to my suggestion. This matter has been before the minister for several weeks, and the situation has become worse and worse in relation to Malaysia.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I just want to suggest to the right hon. gentleman that there ought to be occasions on orders of the day when the right hon. gentleman should consider that he has responsibilities, which I do not think he fully discharges.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a supplementary question of the Secretary of State for External Affairs with regard to Malaysia. Are the press reports correct which state that the government of Malaysia is understood to have made an urgent request to Canada for military and economic aid in its struggle against Indonesia? The minister seemed to indicate that there was a time lag involved here, with some party coming up from Washington. Has there been an urgent request, and what has been Canada's response?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is no time lag. My hon. friend is referring to a story which appeared in one of the leading Canadian newspapers this morning. There has been no request made beyond the request made by the Tunku when he was here three weeks ago. I may say that my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce, when he was in Kuala Lumpur the other day at the commonwealth economic conference, had further consultations with the government of Malaysia along the lines which were discussed between the prime minister of that country and the representatives of the government of Canada a few weeks ago.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I then direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Did he at that conference give as prompt a reply in respect of aid from Canada as was apparently given by other nations of the commonwealth to Malaysia?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I spoke to the ministers of the government of Malaysia along exactly the lines indicated by the Secretary of State for External Affairs.

speechtext:

Perhaps it might be useful to explain a little of what this system is and what has been done in the recent episode concerning the siren.
As hon. members know, there are 31 sirens in the Ottawa-Hull metropolitan area, and these are controlled centrally at the federal warning centre at Carp. There is one main circuit from Carp to the Bell Telephone exchange in Ottawa, and from the exchange there are circuits to individual sirens. These circuits are all leased from the Bell Telephone Company, and the federal warning officer is responsible for activating the sirens in an emergency. There are visible and audible means in the warning centre to show when the sirens have been activated.
All sirens in the metropolitan area started sounding at 14.29 hours on Saturday, September 5, 1964. They were not activated by the federal warning officer, and Bell Telephone informed the department that the sirens were activated by a short circuit in the circuit between Carp and the Bell Telephone exchange, which was caused by a cable being damaged by shotgun pellets. There was no time lost in advising the Department of National Defence and the Bell Telephone Company of what happened, and the subsequent delay in deactivating the circuits was caused by the complexity of the circuits within the Bell Telephone system, so it was not until 15.01 hours that the sirens stopped sounding.
I may also inform the house that the directorate of signals is undertaking a comprehensive investigation of the procedures to be adopted in the case of accidental soundings, with a view to reducing the time lag in

Inquiries of the Ministry deactivating the circuits. Further, I may add that in the pamphlet, "Eleven Steps to Survival" it is set out that it the sirens are sounded the first thing the public should do is turn on their radios, and if the air waves are carrying no special announcement then they can conclude it is a false alarm.

The house resumed from Tuesday, September 8, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pearson:
That the government be authorized to take such steps as may be necessary to establish officially as the flag of Canada a flag embodying the emblem proclaimed by His Majesty King George V on November 21, 1921-three maple leaves conjoined on one stem-in the colours red and white then designated for Canada, the red leaves occupying a field of white between vertical sections of blue on the edges of the flag.
And the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Diefenbaker and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Churchill.

When the house rose at 10.30 last night we were dealing with the attitude of the government toward this particular legislation, and I was
Canadian Flag
expressing some concern over the fact that from numerous sources we have heard the theory advanced that because they know they are faced with a majority of votes the opposition should simply offer token resistance to the motion which is now before the house and permit the issue to come to a vote. I expressed the view that though this might end the debate here in the House of Commons it would certainly not amount to a satisfactory solution as far as the Canadian people are concerned.
The Minister without Portfolio had some interesting observations to make last night on this aspect. The Prime Minister himself offered a suggestion, and it was contained as well in part of the speech made by the leader of the New Democratic party, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam.
It seems to me that with an issue of this nature, an issue that contains as much emotion as this does, there is a great deal more involved than simply allowing the question to come to a vote and letting the vote decide. What is involved here in something far deeper, namely the question of producing a flag that will be satisfactory to people all across Canada. In this respect, Mr. Speaker, there appeared on Saturday, July 11 of this year an editorial in the Winnipeg Tribune which I think deals very fully with this subject, and I should like to place it on the record. It is entitled "Parliament and people" and says:
How political are Canadians?
A foreigner visiting this country must find this a perplexing question. Although the newspapers and air waves provide political news and views in abundance there is a negative undercurrent.
There is a repetitive theme that another election must be avoided at any cost.
Parliament is constantly hectored as a "do nothing" body by the commentators.
Various issues are regarded as being tiresome because they haven't been resolved.
It is difficult to determine whether such views represent the citizen at large or merely are expressions of frustration by the professional political pundits who weary of their task. One thing is certain.
If parliament approved legislation in slap-dash fashion, it would be thoroughly roasted as having abandoned its fundamental responsibility. And undoubtedly the MP's would be reminded again that their $18,000 stipends required them to be more than rubber stamps.
I wholeheartedly agree with that sentiment. The article continues:
It is one of the assets of our parliamentary system that elections can or must be called once a government has lost control or the confidence of the commons. This places a minority government in a delicate position which can only be maintained by-

Canadian Flag
introducing legislation deemed necessary and desirable by the other factions.
No matter what party a citizen may endorse, his first political allegiance should be given to parliament. The present government's uncertain grasp of this basic political philosophy unfortunately has obscured this for many in the conduct of the flag debates. Pushing the flag bill to an extremity and with indecent haste, the government attempts to cover its own ineptitude by charging its opponents with obstructionism.
This charge appeals to those who like quick uncomplicated decisions. The assumption, however, that parliament is supposed to present only token resistance to a government has no validity in our political system.
Then it goes on to say:
Even though the flag bill couldn't rate any better than priority No. 10,000 in matters that require attention-apart from Mr. Pearson's curious obsession-it certainly has become a stumbling block. The government lost its one chance of having this dealt with in relatively dispassionate terms when it renounced the free vote. Despite this gross error, compounded by the desperate two-flag and two-anthem amendments, we still must hope that parliament somehow will untangle the government without resorting to an election.
The elements of the flag dispute are too vague for articulation on the hustings. If Canadians truly are tired of it as a topic while it is in parliament, it isn't likely to strike a higher or nobler chord on the campaign trail. But despite this, those in parliament who oppose either the proposed new flag or the dragooning tactics employed by the government must, in all conscience, employ whatever restraint they can against arbitrary legislation in the interest of the public.
The people of Canada did not demand that this matter should be resolved at this time. And even most of those who approved Mr. Pearson's design hoped for something more conciliatory than his "stand or fall" ultimatum. At the present stage of this contretemps, the government and not parliament is the obstructionist.
Canadians may get tired of any government but God help us when we get tired of parliament.
I think this sums up very concisely the point of view I was attempting to express last evening. This raises the question of why all this haste has been employed in attempting to ram this legislation through the House of Commons. In the first place the Prime Minister and a number of his colleagues on the other side of the house have stated that this was a solemn commitment made to the Canadian people. I can think of a good many other commitments that were a great deal more solemn than this one. I will not go into detail or try to enumerate them, because hon. members opposite have been reminded of them on several occasions.
It is said that this solemn commitment was given, in effect, in reply to a question asked by a reporter at a press conference in Winnipeg. I rather think it was more of an afterthought, or perhaps the Prime Minister at that time seized upon the opportunity to

please somebody. But certainly, Mr. Speaker, it is difficult to imagine that this represents a solemn commitment when it did not even appear in most ol the campaign literature distributed by the Liberal party during the last election campaign.
The Minister of Transport the other day attempted to shed some light on this situation when he quoted an excerpt from a television broadcast by the present Prime Minister in 1960. He attempted to use this as an example of a solemn commitment the Prime Minister had made at that time. It might have been the statement that was made, but I wonder how it stands up in the face of the theory advanced in this house the other day by the Postmaster General, since at that time the present Prime Minister was in the opposition.
This whole affair, right from the time it was introduced at the Legion convention early in April until today, has been a story of bumbling and mismanagement on the part of this government. As a result national unity in this country has reached the lowest ebb in our history. At the present time we have this situation. We have one group of people ardently supporting the retention of the red ensign as Canada's national flag, and we have another group that supports the maple leaf flag. But I think within these two extremes we have a large majority of Canadians who are sincerely hoping this parliament can produce a distinctive Canadian flag.
I think it is the responsibility of this parliament to do so. It cannot be done by simply calling for a vote on this issue, because we know what will be the result of a vote. To allow it to come to a vote would in my opinion simply be an abdication of our responsibility as an opposition. The problem of national unity would not be resolved; in fact it is my opinion that it would be complicated even further. We would have dissension from one end of this country to the other if this matter were permitted to come to a vote.
As I see it, the only solution is to follow the suggestion that was made originally by the hon. member for Edmonton West, then yesterday by the leader of the New Democratic party, and by others in this house, and refer this question to a committee for decision. Once the committee had brought in its recommendation in a spirit of compromise, the spirit with which they would begin their hearings in a sincere effort to produce a flag, I believe a flag could be produced that would be acceptable to Canadians across this country. I do not think it is possible to produce a flag that would be acceptable to everybody, but

I do believe that if this procedure were followed we could produce a flag that will not carry with it all the recriminations, bitterness and hatred that has characterized this debate. I sincerely hope that the parties in this house can get together and produce that kind of flag. In my opinion it can be done.

Mr. Speaker, I must confess it is with some hesitation that I rise to take part in this debate which has been going on for quite some time, because most of the points one could dwell on have already been made very successfully by previous speakers. However, since I have been invited to voice my opinion, I shall do so this afternoon in all sincerity and I do hope that, in so doing I shall not offend anybody.
The present debate seems to be causing a great deal of confusion and concern in the minds of people, and I do not think any issue has raised such heated discussions throughout the country in the past several years. One has but to read the editorials in Canadian newspapers to realize just how strong a feeling of frustration seems to have come over public opinion as a result of this parliament's inability to reach a decision and give our country a national emblem, something which the great majority of Canadians have been asking for quite a number of years already.
Personally, when I go back to my riding for the week end, like most hon. members I am asked these questions. What is happening in Ottawa? When will we have a flag? Will you settle that question? How will you get out of that deadlock? As a member from Quebec, I must say that this debate is giving rise to strong apprehensions among the moderate element in my province and what worries our people most is the damage that some stands and some speeches can really do to Canadian unity.
I know that national unity has become a rather trite expression and that a lot of people are tired of that old cliche but just the same, whether we want it or not, national unity remains the backbone of our development and an absolute necessity in a country like ours.
Mr. Speaker, I know that during this debate, in speeches from all sides of the house, appeals have been made for national unity, many professions of faith have been made in favour of national unity, so much so that I wonder if those professions of faith and state-
Canadian Flag
ments of love are not in fact stifling national unity.
This reminds me of a historical incident which happened in 1862. While Paris was besieged and the city was in dire poverty, famine drove people to eat dogs, cats and other animals of that kind. Now, there was a poor man of Paris named Chavette who had a dog called Medor, his only faithful friend. The time came when Chavette had to eat his friend Medor. While eating his dog, he would place each bone in Medor's plate and when he was finished, looking at the dog's plate, he said: It is too bad that Medor is not here; it would have such a good meal.
The same attitude is taken with respect to national unity. While paying lip service to national unity we let it crumble, and the day may come if the situation deteriorates, when all that will be left will be the skeleton of national unity, and then we shall say: Poor national unity; we would have been so pleased to re-examine it.
Mr. Speaker, where are we going with the situation which prevails now? Are we not running the risk of deepening a division which certainly should not exist in our country? As members of the Canadian parliament, we have a responsibility to this country which extends from sea to sea and it is our duty not to let this difficult situation get any worse.
I will not say the situation is serious because I do not want to be pessimistic. However, I must certainly acknowledge that it is complicated. If, in the province of Quebec, French Canadians are taking a stand which speaks well for the future not only of the province but of the whole of Canada, it must be said that such a reawakening is often spoiled by extremists. In fact, the efforts of the moderate elements in my province are often misunderstood by my friends from the other provinces. There have been heated exchanges between the two groups these past few years, but our politicians, our faculty members, our businessmen, our great newspapermen, etc. have also made fine efforts to bring the two elements closer together.
This debate and, especially, the present stalemate should not be allowed to place parliament and the whole country in an untenable position.
Both parties seem to have taken irreversible stands and the division is becoming more pronounced every day.
I think that both parties delude themselves.
At any rate, the supporters of the three maple leaf flag are deluding themselves with

Canadian Flag
the thought that their design will be adopted without closure. In my opinion, it is a delusion. It is also a delusion for the supporters of the red ensign to believe that it can be maintained without resorting to an endless filibuster.
For my part I was ready to accept the three maple leaf design, as were thousands of Canadians. However, I must admit that the right hon. Prime Minister could not have acted more clumsily than he did in the circumstances, first of all by requesting a confidence vote on the flag issue and afterwards, in conjunction with his supporters, by making this emblem a party symbol, and, finally, by endeavouring to impose the union jack when nobody had requested it.
The supporters of the red ensign are certainly justified to express their opinion, but I do not think that exaggerated outbursts of emotions will settle anything.
Hon. members have so often used the words "great principle"; they have appealed to principle so much that I wondered whether they were not parodying that sally of Aristide Briand: "Rest on your principles, rest on them the most you can; if you rest on them long enough, they will eventually yield".
Mr. Speaker, there has been undoubtedly excesses of language, but I believe that they have gone beyond the thought of the speaker. However, this has made us realize that such a debate could carry us on delicate grounds.
Both delusions-closure and filibuster- nurtured by both parties must be dispelled in both cases: otherwise parliament as an institution will certainly be affected. A compromise must be reached by all means. Besides, compromise is the whole history of Canada. The very existence of this country is due to a compromise, and its future rests also on compromise, understanding and sacrifices accepted on both sides.
Several compromises have been put forward, but I feel that there is a very simple one which is actually recognized by almost all members. When a measure is at the same time wholeheartedly supported by the Toronto Star, Montreal's Le Devoir, the Montreal Gazette and the former premier of Ontario, Mr. Frost, it can be concluded that it is a compromise acceptable throughout the country.
As far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, I am in favour of a flag with only one maple leaf, instead of the flag bearing three maple leaves which is now proposed. In my opinion, a flag with a single maple leaf would be supported by the majority of Canadians.
[Mr. BalcerJ
I do not want to propose any particular design, because I know that my friend the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Vincent) has put forward a flag designed, I must admit, by my brother-in-law.
I feel that I would put myself in a somewhat awkward situation if I were to propose the flag designed by my brother-in-law; nevertheless, I wish him good luck.
Personally, I am ready to accept a flag with a single maple leaf as the symbol of Canada.
I should like to point out that if I support the design with a single maple leaf it is not because the symbol is exclusive to Quebec but because it is a symbol of Canada as a whole.. I would even go so far as saying that it is more a symbol of English Canada than it is of French Canada.
As a second flag, signifying our membership in the commonwealth, I suggest that the red ensign be substituted for the union jack. I appreciate that to suddenly abandon the red ensign would be a much too quick transition for some hon. members and that the shock would perhaps be too sudden. But why could we not adopt the red ensign instead of the union jack, since the acceptance of the union jack as a second flag is so ridiculous that the matter is not even worth discussing.
It would be tragic if, after such a long debate, we could not have a truly distinctive Canadian flag, and that is why a compromise is so essential. We should bear in mind that it is the young people of today who want a distinctive and essentially Canadian flag, the youth in every province of Canada.
I should like to point out to hon. members that they need have no fear, this is not a concession to Quebec, but a concession to the Canada of 1964.
When I go back in my riding and meet young French Canadians expressing separatist feelings, I tell them, as all hon. members do, to be a little more Canadian, in short, true Canadians.
A few weeks ago, one of them told me: "The rest of Canada is asking us to be Canadians and nothing more, to think only in terms of one Canada. Well, why do they still want to keep the union jack which is the emblem of another country?" I think it is worth while to work together in 1964 and do something that is fundamentally Canadian.
I know that it will undoubtedly call for a measure of sacrifice from some older members and that it will be with a degree of nostalgia that they will see another flag replace the red ensign. Unfortunately those are the facts of life.

As a matter of fact, it must be remembered that one day Sir Winston Churchill said: I will never preside over the dismemberment of the British empire. At that time he was wildly applauded, but times have changed. Today if those same Englishmen who applauded Churchill's patriotic speech were asked to take back India, Pakistan or Ceylon, I feel that they would be quite reluctant to do so.
In the course of the debate, several members have stressed the fact that the red ensign was the flag under which our Canadian forces fought in the last war. They were right, and their respect for it is still perfectly justified; our children and our grandchildren will also have every reason to respect it.
Mr. Speaker, I served in the Canadian navy, and let me tell you that if there was anything at that time that burned up Canadian sailors more than anything else it was to be mistaken for British sailors. What they wanted at all costs was to be recognized everywhere as Canadians, purely and simply. That is why one day, as we entered the ports of the royal navy in England, some ordinary Canadian seamen went up and painted a big red maple leaf on their ship's funnel. Those men were not French Canadians any more than they were English Canadians. They were just plain Canadian sailors who were proud to be Canadians and for whom the maple leaf was a distinctive Canadian emblem.
One of the greatest thrills we felt when Canadian ships entered an English port or joined a convoy was to hear the sailors aboard the other ships welcome us with those words: Hello Canada, because of the maple leaf on our funnels.
Mr. Speaker, this tradition, which was established in the navy during the war was maintained and was never criticized by anybody.
As far as I am concerned, at the time I was minister of transport, when colour had to be given to our coastguard, I insisted that a large red maple leaf be painted on the white funnels. Up to now, I have received no criticism at all.
Mr. Speaker, when the three maple leaf flag was introduced, I supported it without any reservation. I saw in it a factor of Canadian unity. I must say that, like many Canadians, I was disappointed by the partisanship which accompanied its introduction. Unfortunately, it has become somewhat too much the emblem of one party.
On the other hand, like many Conservatives, in the province of Quebec in particular, I
Canadian Flag
must recognize that the stand of the majority of my party also disappointed me, and I need not insist further on this matter.
I am, therefore, suggesting the immediate appointment of a committee in order to determine the choice of a flag.
Personally, as I was saying a while ago, I think that a single maple leaf on that flag would be acceptable. And I suggest that we keep the red ensign as a flag commemorating our membership in the commonwealth.
However, I must say that if such a committee is appointed, I personally believe we should insist on the majority rule, provided it represents two thirds of the members of that committee. I suggest two thirds, because if one studies all the new constitutions set up over the past century, one realizes that when decisions of importance for modern and contemporary history have to be made in any of those countries, a two thirds majority is the maximum required.
It seems, therefore, that this would be reasonable in the circumstances and would provide a flag chosen by the majority.
Mr. Speaker, what I fear most about this debate is that it will result in racial strife.
Sincere Canadians want parliament to maintain its prestige, and I feel we should co-operate in building a fine Canada where it is good to live.
Mr. Speaker, I hope that the compromise idea will prevail and that the house will take a decision without further delay.
As for me, I am opposed to a referendum, as I am against a general election on this kind of issue. I believe that both could result in a division within the country and could cause wrongs that would last much too long.
Undoubtedly, the flag debate has had interesting aspects, but I think that in the interest of national unity, it is time to stop paying lip service to that unity and start working towards it; let us give the country an essentially Canadian flag which will be respected from coast to coast.

Mr. Speaker, I was not supposed to speak this afternoon, but following the speeches which have just been delivered I feel that we will reach an agreement. If everyone cooperates and refrains from playing on emotions, I think that we will reach the agreement so ardently desired by the Canadian people.
I do not wish to extend the debate further, but I simply want to add a few words, so that we may bring to an end that marathon

Canadian Flag
debate which we have been patiently following for more than 20 days.
During the past week especially, our party has been trying by every possible means to work out an agreement. Even yesterday, we came within a hair's breadth of succeeding. However, if that has led to the suggestions made today or the agreement which we hope will soon be reached, our efforts will not have been in vain.
Mr. Speaker, we are confronted today with a contest that I would not qualify as national, but as a clash between two parties, perhaps well intended, but which are certainly too much taken by the ambition to win in turn some honours.
First of all the government presented us with a three maple leaf flag design. Everyone admits even today, even the hon. members on the government side, that if the government had handled the matter differently, if it had moved a motion to set up a committee for consideration of a flag design which would have received the approval of this parliament as a whole, the design presented then would have been undoubtedly more national in character than the one we now have before us.
Therefore, I blame a little the Liberal government which probably thought it was doing the right thing but certainly blundered in introducing a flag design the way it did. Later the government went back on its decision and rectified a little its mistake by making concessions.
Here I must commend the government for its broadmindedness when it was willing to recognize its past mistakes and to suggest to the house the establishment of a committee and a free vote on this flag business; I think those were the two stumbling blocks in the presentation of its flag.
I say that it was really accused, these days, of having introduced a Liberal flag. After all, it has almost become the general idea in the opposition in this parliament that the way of introducing it reflects too much the partisan spirit and not enough the national spirit. That is why we wish with all our hearts the national spirit to prevail in this parliament, and it is only then that we can reach a reasonable agreement.
On the other hand we note that the conservative party has reversed its policy, as was proper. Nor am I ready to blame completely the Tory party for its change of policy as a political party, two parties facing one another, one introducing its flag and the other changing its policy with another flag.

We must not forget that today, if the Conservative party just reversed their stand on the red ensign, they would not have unanimous agreement of their members any more, by the way, than the Liberals had 100 per cent agreement of their own members.
99 per cent.
We saw members of both parties speak in this house against their own leader.
Only one, and and that is why we say 99 per cent.

They say there was only one, but that is without counting those who will not speak up. It is for that reason that if both old line parties had held the necessary caucus in the first place, they would have reached an agreement on some design or on some criticism and we would have probably avoided this marathon. This means that this marathon was certainly brought about by failures on both sides.
From red ensign supporters, we heard pathetic speeches. I would not call them historic speeches because for us, the red ensign has no historical character, since it is only temporary.
And besides, it is not patriotic.
The red ensign was accepted by parliament only conditionally and temporarily until there would be a really distinctive flag which would be our national flag.
Hear, hear.

When I hear the Conservatives say "We fought under that flag", I admit that they fought under the colours of that flag. But then, they must recognize that they only fought under a temporary flag.
I heard another Conservative member say: We taught our children that the red ensign is our national flag. Well, Mr. Speaker, if they did, they taught their children a lie because we in the province of Quebec taught our children the truth, namely that the red ensign, which we respect just the same, is only the temporary flag of Canada until we have our distinctive national flag. That is the truth, Mr. Speaker.
We always made it a point to teach the new generations the true meaning of our national policy. Even if it is said in this parliament that our children were taught that the red ensign is the national flag, I say and will always say that it is false, that it is a flag that was chosen to be used by our

troops on the battlefields, but it is not a national flag, only a temporary one.
I heard someone else say that the threeleaved flag was commercial in design. Since the red ensign is the flag of the British merchant marine, I wonder which of the two is more commercial. How can anyone say that one is less commercial than the other?
Mr. Speaker, I refer to those few statements made by the hon. members on both sides of the house only to show that they could not have been serious when they made such claims. I fail to understand how a Conservative, regardless of whether he is a French Canadian, an English speaking Canadian or an immigrant, could seriously seek to prove to the house that the red ensign is our national flag. No one could seriously do so.
I cannot imagine either that the Conservatives are serious when they ask for a referendum on the proposed flag. Last night, the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napier-ville (Mr. Dupuis) gave us a proof that was lacking up to now. As a matter of fact, some present Conservative members have actually disavowed in 1961 what they advocate today. It means therefore that someone is playing the fool, that there are some jokers in the house. We want to put an end to this sort of thing, because I do not think any responsible member wishes to make of this house a stage for make-believe. Every Canadian feels that this monumental farce should be stopped.
It is said that the right of free speech must be respected. I agree, Mr. Speaker, but when someone has expressed his views once, even twice or three times, I feel that when he speaks for the fourth time he is abusing the right of free speech. The farmers in our ridings call that sheer foolishness and say that those who are responsible for such abuses deserve to be sent to hospital.
I think that it is time for the Liberal government to face up to its responsibilities. If we could assume the government's responsibility, we would readily do so.
It appears that the motion we intend to introduce was irregular. Now, we have to amend it before introducing it. On the other hand after consulting experienced politicians, I learned that a motion to set up a committee of the house can be introduced only by a minister, and not by a private member.
Such a motion has to be introduced by a minister and that is why I rise today to demand that the Liberal government assume its responsibilities and introduce that motion concerning the setting up of the kind of com-
Canadian Flag
mittee which was suggested yesterday, a time limit being specified for the presentation of the committee's report and for the discussion of that report.
The government may rest assured that for the sake of peace and unity in this country we will wholeheartedly support such a motion. I would even go so far as to say that if, one day, it is obliged to impose closure, we will support it in order to safeguard Canadian unity, because the more we go along the present way, the more we deepen the chasm which is dividing Canadians. We must end this division and I am sure that we shall never reach any agreement by carrying on with this marathon. As a matter of fact the events of the last few days have proved that we could go on discussing this matter for another three months without attaining any results; instead of going forward we are going backward.
We must absolutely settle this matter and the only solution, in my opinion, is the one suggested by the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer), speaking once more on behalf of his party, to the effect that a committee be set up to select a flag that would be approved by the majority of members. I say that the house is responsible for the choice of a distinctive national flag for Canada, and it should be done through a committee that would sit for 60 days, whose report could be discussed later for four, five or six days, that is for a determined period, when the majority could vote at last, once and for all on the distinctive national flag issue. I say a distinctive national flag, not two and not the red ensign, because I do not see why Canada, like all the other countries of the commonwealth, would not have her own distinctive national flag in the British commonwealth of nations. Can you find any other country of the commonwealth who needs two flags to indicate its participation in the commonwealth? If we are unable to fly our distinctive national flag, then we are not worthy of a flag, we do not deserve the name of Canadian nation.
We support the idea of a flag being chosen by a vote taken after six days of discussion on the report made to the house by a committee established for that purpose. I ask the ministers to introduce this motion this afternoon if possible or tomorrow at the latest so that we can put an end to this stupid marathon.

Mr. Speaker,
I did not really intend to take part in the debate, as I wanted, if possible, to avoid

Canadian Flag
delaying the enactment of legislation on the national flag. But, 25 years ago this year, under circumstances similar to those we have here today and just a month before the arrival of Their Majesties King George VI and Queen Elizabeth at the Toronto legislature, I had the opportunity, as a French Canadian representative to rise on a motion to present Their Majesties with an address engraved on metal. At that time, after having heard various members who preceded me speak of the importance of making our Canadian children realize the significance of the British empire, and of our attachment to the commonwealth, I could not but remark that I very much deplored the fact that, in our Canadian schools we did not try to teach our children the true history of Canada, but rather the history of the British empire and that the true history of Canada should be based on the achievement of our forefathers, and the work accomplished by our fathers and grandfathers.
I added that one of the most important deficiencies on the occasion of the visit of Their Majesties was due to the fact that they would be welcomed in this country under various flags, as Canada did not have a distinctive national one. I mentioned that in the maritime provinces, the Scottish flag would be flown and in Quebec the tricolour as there was no provincial flag at the time, while the union jack would be hoisted in Ontario and, in the western provinces, probably the red ensign. I, incidentally, deplored the fact that, just the year before the Canadian scouts attending a jamboree in England were the only troops without a flag, some of them having adopted the union jack, while others were flying the red ensign. And, I defy the Conservatives to deny this statement.
I deplored those facts, adding that I was not making a speech on the flag with a view to the immediate adoption of a national flag, but that I wanted to express my views and launch the idea, so that I might, if the Lord does grant me a few more years, see a really distinctive flag being chosen for Canada.
Following that speech in the house, I received hundreds of letters from The Native Sons of Canada, an organization that is probably known to all members of the house. In these letters, coming from everywhere, from Halifax to Vancouver, I was asked to give a series of lectures on a national flag. I gave to all those letters the same answer, that is that I had not raised the question in view of the immediate adoption of a flag,

but mainly to give rise to an idea in the public mind so that some day, we could have a really distinctive national flag.
This afternoon, the hon. member for Three Rivers was extraordinarily outspoken, in my opinion. I gather that for a member of parliament who has occupied several positions in his party it must be quite a performance to have to state in the house that he deplores the stand taken by the majority of his party's members. Therefore, I congratulate him for the courage he has shown.
I congratulate also the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere (Mr. Paul) for the speech he made a while ago and more particularly for his remarks on the position of his leader with regard to the flag issue.
Mr. Speaker, I wish with heart and hand the right hon. Leader of the Opposition would study seriously the situation in which he puts his party at the present time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Would you congratulate the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan)?
Mi. Habel: In answer to that question I would say that even in the best of families there are black sheep.
Oh, oh.

He has a right to his opinion and he is just as stubborn as you are.

I was saying, Mr. Speaker, that the right hon. Leader of the Opposition should realize that there is a limit to compromise. If, on the one hand, the Prime Minister has shown some good will in already accepting a compromise, the Leader of the Opposition ought to understand that he too is under some obligation to this country and that he is duty bound to promote national unity.
As the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) so aptly put it, let us stop referring to national unity while undermining it with fiery speeches.
Let us proceed with a serious examination of the flag issue and allow the elected representatives of the people to vote, so that this question, like the other matters concerning the Canadian people, can be settled by a majority vote in this house.

A great deal has been said about this flag issue. I am one of those who have said a few words. I could point out to you, Mr. Speaker, as I did

earlier in this debate, that we need only look under our desks to see the amount of literature, the number of words, the number of pages of words spoken on this subject.
As members of the official opposition we have been criticized both here in the house, and, I will admit it frankly, in other places for the attitude we have taken. We have sat in our seats and listened to the debate. We have listened to speeches made in other quarters of the house-speeches made by members opposite, by the leaders of other parties, by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and by other members of the government.
Only yesterday we listened to certain arguments put forward by the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette), who is very seldom in his seat. Today as usual he is not in his seat. The hon. member took up a great deal of the time of this house in speaking in particular about absenteeism in reference to this debate. An hon. member who speaks about other members being absent should certainly have something to back up what he says. The hon. member for Villeneuve put this forward in the form of a challenge, and in return I would like to challenge him: If he wants to rise in his place as a member of this house and criticize other members for not being here, certainly he should be present himself at times. I could be a little more personal in this regard, Mr. Speaker, but I realize that members of this house should not adopt that attitude.
The hon. member to whom I have referred yesterday said something to the effect that French Canadians will not swallow this sort of thing. He also mentioned that a person in a particular firm in my constituency of Lethbridge indicated his preference for a certain design of flag. This person also had something to say on whether or not there should be a plebiscite, but I will not go into that matter because I realize the question has yet to be settled.
I would remind the hon. member for Villeneuve that much earlier in this debate, on one of the days when he was not present, I reminded the house that in my constituency there were many more than just 1 per cent in favour of the particular design that is before the house in the resolution put forward by the government. As a matter of fact, I pointed out that according to my information, correspondence I have received, and the newspaper polls, 8 per cent of the people in my constituency were in favour of the particular design the government has brought forth in their resolution. I would repeat, not just
Canadian Flag
1 per cent but 8 per cent of a great number of people. I also pointed out that there were more people in favour of a design containing a single maple leaf. I even mentioned the percentage, which was 16 per cent. That is twice as many people as are in favour of the design proposed by the government. Mr. Speaker, we have listened to an hon. member of this house emphasizing the absenteeism of members. I would like to repeat, by way of emphasis, that those people who speak about absenteeism should be here more often. As I mentioned earlier, we have also listened to the leaders of and spokesmen for the different parties in this house. They have spoken with complete sincerity with regard to flag designs, and so on. I heard an hon. member the other day-I think it was the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), who is not in his seat at the moment either-
He is at the thinkers conference.

Well, wherever and however, he is not in his seat at the moment. If my memory is correct, that hon. member said the Canadian ensign only flew at headquarters level. According to the information I have, the Canadian ensign flew at every victory on the field, as well as at defeats; it was not just flown at headquarters. I could be wrong, Mr. Speaker, but this is the fact according to my information.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Hon. George Hees could not then have been at any battles.
I hear an hon. member opposite interjecting. I would be glad to resume my seat if he would get on his feet and repeat his interjection.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I simply said that Hon. George Hees could not have been at any battles, because he said he did not see the red ensign during all his years overseas.

I am very glad that the hon. member has made this interjection, or asked this question, or whatever it is. According to my information, what I have said is correct. If you delve a little more deeply into history, and in particular the history of Hon. George Hees, you will find that although he may not have seen the ensign, it was there. And he does not have to apologize for his actions. I could produce many people, affidavits and letters with regard to the actions of Hon. George Hees overseas. Many, many of them were very happy to have that

Canadian Flag
kind of man to lead them back when they were pinned down without an officer.
Hear, hear.

And it was on a voluntary basis. As I have said, Mr. Speaker, if you want to look through history you will find that the ensign was flying at that battle, on the field.
A great deal has been said about the recognition of Canada's flag, whether it is appropriate, whether it is legal, and all sorts of things. In this connection I should like to relate a personal experience. I was walking in front of the west block a week ago, and beside me was an American tourist. We saw the flags of the commonwealth flying in front of that building. The American tourist had no trouble recognizing Canada's flag; he was proud of it and said, "We recognize it readily and easily, and we are proud to have you as a neighbour".
I have spoken previously in this debate but I do not apologize at all for that, Mr. Speaker. I am quite proud to be a member of the Conservative party, the official opposition in this house, that is responsible for this issue being debated at the moment. We have been criticized a great deal in this connection, particularly in the house; nevertheless the attitude and the approach of this party in the debate has been to discuss certain designs and ways and means of bringing about a distinctive Canadian flag. As I said earlier, I am proud to be a member of the party which is really responsible for bringing this debate before the house and to this point today.
I should like to put on record, if I may, some words which were uttered on January 23, 1961, page 1318 of Hansard, by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Horner). Much has been said about this, and indeed said only yesterday by a minister of the crown, a member of the government who, I am sorry to say, is not in his place at the moment. On this occasion the hon. member for Acadia referred to this question:
Are you in favour of a truly distinctive Canadian flag? That is the first question that should be answered. If the answer is overwhelmingly in the affirmative then the government in power should have the courage to decide on a truly distinctive flag. It could establish a committee such as the one that met in 1945-46, if it wishes. I am convinced that those who expressed themselves in the census as wanting a flag would accept the design on which the government of the day decided.
That brings up another point, Mr. Speaker, although I think the house is already aware of it. Hon. members are realizing, and have done over the last few days, that the flag design proposed by the government was not

considered by the government. I am beginning to wonder whether the government had an opportunity even to discuss this particular design. I am beginning to wonder whether the government-and by the government I mean the cabinet-did have such an opportunity. I am also wondering, Mr. Speaker, whether this design was presented to the government, or if you wish the cabinet, in the same way as it might have been presented to the caucus of the government party and in the same way as it was presented to this House of Commons-"This is it; take it or leave it".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: It was not, for one thing.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: No, it was not presented; that is correct. That is what the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) said.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Well, he does not know what he is talking about.

I did not say that it was or that it was not. I only said I was beginning to wonder. As I said earlier, I am very proud to speak today as a member of the party which has brought the debate to this point, but all I said was that I was beginning to wonder.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Then stop wondering, because it had been discussed in caucus many times.
I would be glad to have any information which is available, and I will gladly give up part of my time if the hon. member wants to get up and explain-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: You might as well; you are not saying anything.
-and to put his remarks on record.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: They are on record.
Would the hon. member like to do that?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: He is afraid to.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: My remarks are on record.

Well, I hope your remarks are on record. I am not trying to promote any sort of controversy; I am merely saying what is sincerely and honestly in my mind, and I have said that I am wondering about certain matters. Furthermore I am wondering whether there was not a deal between the Prime Minister of Canada and the prime minister of Quebec.
Shame.

If the hon. member has the information I would be glad to have it. I am

saying that I am beginning to wonder, Mr. Speaker.
You are insinuating.
There is no insinuation whatever. I am beginning to wonder about this, and if anyone wants to put me straight I would be glad to yield the floor and have him put the facts on record.

Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) has just said from his seat that the hon. member is lying. The remarks previously made by the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) are in direct contradiction to what the hon. member for Kootenay East is now saying. The members on this side of the house would very much appreciate it if that hon. member would get up on his feet and put on the record the remarks he has just made from his seat.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if I understand the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Maclnnis), he stated that I had inferred that the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Gundlock) was lying. I did not use such a term, and I have never used such a term in the house. When the hon. member was wandering, or wondering-I do not know which was the word he used-whether this matter had been discussed in caucus, I cannot say what happened in cabinet because that is beyond my province but I can certainly tell him that this matter was discussed on several occasions in caucus before presentation.

Mr. Speaker, I accept the hon. member's explanation that he did not say that the hon. member was lying, but if the hon. member has any contribution to make, I would appreciate it if he would get to his feet before making it, so that it can be understood by members on this side. While I am on my feet I would also ask him to consider whether or not he is now saying that he is calling the hon. member for York-Humber a liar.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Well, that does not trouble me too much. I have made a statement which is a correct statement. If it differs from the views of others then that is a matter for determination.

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I believe the actions of the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) during the last few minutes have been clearly
Canadian Flag
out of order. Citation 143 of Beauchesne states:
Whilst a member is addressing the house, no one has a right to interrupt him by putting a question to him, or by making or demanding an explanation.
During the last few minutes the hon. member for Kootenay East has been trying to interrupt the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Gundlock) by asking him questions, making explanations, and so on. Under the rules of the house and under the citation to which I have just referred no member has the right to do this except with the express consent of the member who has the floor. The citation goes on:
A member will, at times, allow such interruptions through a sense of courtesy to another, but it is entirely at the option of the member in possession of the floor to give way or not to an immediate explanation.
The hon. member for Lethbridge did offer to give way to the hon. member for Kootenay East if he wanted to get on his feet and make a speech giving his views on some of the matters the hon. member for Lethbridge was discussing. I noticed very clearly that the member for Kootenay East did not accept that offer, and therefore I think he ought to abide by these rules and allow the hon. member for Lethbridge, who I think has the right to make his own speech, to continue his speech uninterrupted.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. I think there is some merit in the point of order raised by the hon. member for Medicine Hat. One of the rules of this house is that an hon. member who is speaking has the right to make his remarks without interruption. Perhaps I should point out to the hon. member for Lethbridge that some of the interruptions which were made from the opposite side of the house may have been provoked by his insistance, or invitation, that someone should stand up and make a speech, and that he would then yield the floor. If the hon. member did yield the floor I would have some doubt as to whether he would again have leave to continue his speech.
Perhaps that hon. member will now continue.

Mr. Speaker, I thank you very much and hope that you will appreciate that I am a new member and probably overstep the rules. I should like to congratulate you for your forbearance, and will make a sincere attempt to comply with your ruling. What I said earlier was said sincerely and

Canadian Flag
with the serious hope that I will be corrected when I need correction.
I should like to read into the record at this time a letter I received only today from an individual who I am sure is not particularly a supporter of mine. This is a very sincere letter written by a Canadian citizen who happens to be one of my constituents. With your permission I shall read this letter into the record and then make some comment in respect of one or two points contained therein. The letter is addressed to me and commences as follows:
Dear Friend and M.P.
I appreciate your letters and information you have mailed at different times. I am willing to give you my opinion on this flag business, which is being very wrongly dealt with by both parties-
I am pleased that this individual did not identify the parties to which he referred, and on that basis perhaps I could excuse my own party, although I will not attempt to do so. The letter then continues:
-and is a disgrace to have spent this whole session the way it been. But I hope this Pearson flag will not be accepted if you have to stay there till next year. The best thing that could be done now is drop the whole flag business till some future and find out if any amount of people... approve...
Then some government that thought more of the country than they did of their policies, could appoint a committee of members from all the parties to choose a new flag. A vote on this flag business will only make more trouble. The side who loses will want to spit on the flag every time they see it. If Pearson forces his three maple leaves on this country he will not get all the blame, you who allow it to happen will get your share of it. A vote on the question will be as bad as-
And the next word is not quite clear. That letter was written by a Canadian citizen in an honest attempt to criticize this house as a whole, and I think it sets out some of the thoughts of many Canadians.
In this house we have all heard a great deal of reference to this flag issue. Only a moment ago a member to my left suggested that Canadians were not doing anything about the situation. As I have said on several previous occasions-one in particular-I think Canadians are doing something about the situation. They are trying very hard to accomplish an understanding throughout this country which will lead to a distinctive Canadian flag. On an earlier occasion I put on record what I thought a distinctive Canadian flag should be. Perhaps I should repeat what I said at that time.
For a variety of worth-while reasons I think we should use the Canadian ensign as a

basic design for a new distinctive flag. Perhaps we could replace the union jack, as it appears on the present ensign, with a complete ensign of reduced size. We would then have approximately three quarters of the entire flag on which could appear a three maple leaf design, or a single maple leaf design which could be red, green or any other desirable colour. Perhaps it would be well to place a sheaf of wheat emblem, or a peace pipe emblem, on the fly of the flag, as I suggested earlier. I have repeated this suggestion, Mr. Speaker, for emphasis.
Over a period of days, weeks, months and even years I have thought about the flag, and it is utterly inconceivable to consider completely abandoning the use of what I refer to as our heritage, as exemplified by our present and legal flag-and it is our legal flag in spite of what some people suggest. Those individuals need only refer to certain orders in council, or to certain portions of Hansard to realize that fact.
Many flag designs have been proposed, Mr. Speaker. I should like to quote from an editorial in the Toronto Telegram of Saturday, August 22 last which I must say, in all fairness and honesty, is not at all complimentary to one party or another. It reads as follows:
The Canadian ensign must not be lowered without the consent of the people.
I realize it may be a little late for this sort of talk, but perhaps not.
No decision of the House of Commons, by free vote or otherwise, to strike our historic ensign and replace it with a pennant of the Prime Minister's choosing can be construed as expressing the consensus of the nation.
This brings me back to what I was saying earlier. Some members opposite took exception when I said I wondered whether the design contained in the resolution in the name of the Prime Minister was really discussed and considered by cabinet and by caucus. With all deference, I really wonder whether this took place. I have innumerable letters here-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker-
-that point out the fact-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Cape Breton South made the assertion that I had called the hon. member for Lethbridge a liar because I said that this matter had been discussed in caucus. I have made the statement while standing in my place, that this matter

was discussed in caucus. There is no longer any reason for the hon. member for Lethbridge to say that he wonders whether it was discussed in the Liberal caucus. I have stated that to be the fact and he must accept my word.

On the question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, probably I should have made myself clearer. Again I have to apologize, because as a new member of the house I sometimes forget certain rules. I should have made it clear earlier that what I was wondering about was whether this matter was discussed by the cabinet and in caucus prior to the House of Commons being presented with the resolution. This is what I was trying to point out but possibly I did not make myself clear. The point I was trying to make was whether members of all parties in the house were confronted with this resolution in the same way as the cabinet and the Liberal caucus were. That is the only point I was trying to make, and I hope the hon. member appreciates that. I neglected to refer to the time. I was reading from an editorial in the Toronto Telegram which goes on to state:
The voice of the people can be heard, on this issue, only through a national plebiscite. None would seriously suggest that all controversial issues before parliament should be resolved by plebiscite or referendum. That is not the way our system works. A government having received its mandate pushes ahead with its legislative program and stakes its life on its success or failure. But the flag issue is different.
If I may deviate for a moment, Mr. Speaker, I agree with this kind of thinking. The government did not have a mandate to bring this particular design before parliament. I challenge the members of the government or any private member opposite to point out to me where the government had a clear mandate, let alone even an implied mandate, from the people of Canada to bring in this particular flag design.
I said earlier that I have a multitude of letters. They are not only from supporters of the party to which I belong but in many cases are from supporters of the government party and in some cases from supporters of the parties to the left. I should like to compliment them at this moment, if I may. Members of the other parties in the house as well as members of the official opposition have contributed a great deal to this debate.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: That is a matter of opinion.

Certainly it is a matter of opinion; it is my opinion. I was only trying to be somewhat gracious in saying that mem-
Canadian Flag
bers of every party in the house have contributed a great deal to this debate. I said earlier and I repeat by way of emphasis that I am proud to be speaking today as a member of the party that has brought the debate to this point. If it is not possible to pay a slight tribute to other parties in the house on occasion, Mr. Speaker, I will refrain from doing so in the future.
Earlier I took some exception to the remarks of a previous speaker from the party to my far left who said that nothing was being done in the country to try to solve the problem. I said earlier in the house and at great length that I thought something was being done. In particular, I referred to the fact that something was being done in the city of Lethbridge in my constituency. I asked the question whether any other city in Canada was doing the same thing. I also pointed out what the consensus was in my constituency with regard to a flag design. I referred to percentage figures. I should like to repeat what I said earlier in the house. Every two weeks during the past school summer holidays the city of Lethbridge has sent 20 high school students to Montreal and has arranged to have 20 Montreal students brought to the homes of the Lethbridge students. This exchange has been going on every two weeks all summer. My constituents have delegated me to say that they are overwhelmingly in favour of the red ensign. I would also express my opinion on certain designs that might be a compromise, but I want to challenge those who say that nothing is being done. I am particularly proud of the fact that my own city is doing something, and I doubt if there is any other city in Canada doing the same thing. This is the kind of thing that will really resolve this question, and there is more involved in this than just the flag design.
This is a question of people living together, a problem we have had since the early days of confederation. I am very proud of our confederation arrangement. It is something which is unique and something we should guard very jealously. My people in my constituency, if I have to put it that way, are working with your people and, as I have said previously, I hope when we use adjectives denoting racial origin in this house it is only in a geographical sense.
We have our differences, the same as members of any Canadian family have their differences. We have our arguments, but I have no doubt that we can work out our differences. I have always tried to defer to your rulings, Mr. Speaker. Quite frankly on this occasion I

Canadian Flag
have tried to attract the attention of hon. members opposite, but I have sincerely and honestly brought these points before the house and in the summary of my speech, if it can be called that, I pointed out that I am quite sure we as Canadians will resolve the issue of a distinctive Canadian flag design.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

During the course of his speech the hon. member said he was wondering whether or not there had been some deal arranged between the Prime Minister and Premier Lesage of Quebec. Has he also been wondering whether a deal was arranged between the Prime Minister and Premier Stanfield of Nova Scotia and the former prime minister of Ontario, Hon. Leslie Frost, who have both said they are in favour of a distinctive flag for Canada?
That is too tricky.
No prompting over there.

I said I was wondering if there had been a deal between the Prime Minister of Canada and the prime minister of Quebec. I only wonder this because there are some things which are becoming very obvious.
How about the question?
I asked the hon. member if he had been wondering whether these other two gentlemen ever made a deal with the Prime Minister?
The simple answer is no, I have not been wondering about that.

Mr. Speaker, I usually try to make my remarks positive, but before I start the main body of my talk I have to make some small criticism of the critics. In this flag debate hon. members, with the exception of those in the Conservative party, whenever they have intervened or interjected have made personal remarks designed to destroy the character of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker). I take exception to this, and I also object to interjections from hon. members opposite. I prefer that they stand and make their speeches.
This character assassination has gone on too long, and if you look behind it you can see the reason for it is very plain. To be old fashioned about it, in other words there are forces of evil at work in the world today.

I am old fashioned enough to believe there is right and wrong in the world today and I am ready to take my stand on what I think is right.
We hear complaints on all sides that we do not have leadership in our country today. I am not going to say whether or not we do have, but I am inclined to believe that we do. I think the standard of public service in Canada today is as high as or higher than it has ever been. I for one am not satisfied to run down parliament, or run down the kind of men who come here. It is a dirty bird that dirties its own nest. I think there are in this house men of courage, men of vision and men of leadership. I am sorry if at any time they appear to be bound by party ties, and if this is so I am sure it is equally true on either side of the house, and in the smaller groups in the corner; but I say with all sincerity that there are dedicated men in all corners of the house.
Sometimes they are misled. Sometimes their theories of government and theories of political need are clouded, and I think that some intellectuals of our country are often responsible for this. I have just read a very meaningful essay by Mr. Scott Symons in Executive magazine. He is a man who is out of politics; he is in charge of the Canadian exhibition at the Toronto museum, and I commend his article to hon. members. He refers to English Canadians, and at the outset I would like to say I do not like using hyphenated words, but there are English Canadians the same as there are French Canadians. One would have hoped that over a period of 97 years we would have learned better, that we would have become simply Canadians, and as an English speaking Canadian and as one of Anglo-Saxon origin I bemoan this.
