The other day I asked for co-operation and consent for our side of the picture. I begged that we do not take a revered symbol from our war memorials. Is this a rabid thing to ask on behalf of the widows and mothers of those who died voluntarily to keep our country free, those who died in the second world war which many of us have already forgotten? But when one refers to this some of our egghead gossips say, "You are trotting out the flag, trying to make yourself a war hero." Mr. Speaker, I was not a war hero. I was an observer most of the time. I spent five and a half years overseas away from my family, and most of the time I was hot fighting. I was one of those Milton spoke about when he said, "They also

serve who only stand and wait." I waited, but I was there. I also had a spot of fighting in Belgium, Holland and Germany.
I want to talk about what happened in 1940. There is something to be learned from history. In case I bore you-
You do.

-let me say there is something to be learned from history. I am not going back to the middle ages, but to 1940. What happened in 1940? Western civilization was scared to death. The Germans had 350 divisions of well armed and well trained men. What were they addicted to?-a narrow nationalism. I hope nobody in this house is devoted to narrow nationalism, either English speaking or French. All right. In 1940 we had a pitiful little army sitting at one end of the Maginot line. The Maginot line was full of people who did not believe in France, and so France fell. Around the right end of that wall, which was only half a wall, came the panzer divisions. And what happened? The pitifully small English speaking army had to run for it. And there they were on the beaches of Dunkirk. What happened then? Yes, I am speaking about the unity of Canada, and if the hon. member does not understand that I am speaking about the unity of Canada I advise him to listen for the next 35 minutes because he may learn some small thing. I believe in the unity of Canada and volunteered, myself, to help preserve that unity; and I would do it again. I am talking about the subamendment, don't you worry. All right; I am talking about leadership, which means unity. Without leadership you have no unity. They had leadership in England in those days. They had a man, King George VI. He was not only a king; he was a real man. He was not afraid to put his Christian faith above everything else. What did he do? He called a national day of prayer; and on May 26, 1940, 365,000 men without arms or anything with which to fight back were gathered on the beaches of Dunkirk. King George put his Christian faith ahead of his royalty and begged the people of England to get down on their knees and pray. And they did; and so did I.
Were you scared?
Yes, I was scared. But I was not so scared that I was not over there. Where was the hon. member who made that interruption from his seat?

I was there.
Canadian Flag

Then you do not have to ask me that question; you were scared, too. I was there. We prayed; and five days later 330,000 fighting men were safe home in England.
This I call a miracle-the miracle of Dunkirk. It came about because we had leadership in England in those days and we had faith in the three Christian crosses which are embodied in our Christian flag. And when France fell, because she did not have faith in herself, where did de Gaulle go? He went to seek the protection of the British flag. Four years later he was able to mass the forces of the free world and return to help deliver France and the rest of Europe from the terror of the nazi regime. Do not call the men who went there fools and cowards. Scared, we may have been, but not cowards-
No one has done that.

I am telling you right now. You say you are as willing to meet me as I am to meet you. Would you like to look at Hansard. It is in Hansard. When I begged you to leave these symbols of our faith on our war memorials to the boys who cannot fight for themselves, what did you say? Only one replied, I admit. Is there anybody else who agrees with him? "We shall rub you off". Is this the way to answer an appeal for unity? "We shall rub you off"-would the gentleman like to get up and explain what he meant? I know who he is, and so do you, Mr. Speaker. The writers of Hansard had the decency to leave his name off the record and I will have the decency to leave his name off, now-"We shall rub you off". There is only one way to deal with that kind of talk. But is this not a chamber in which to discuss a subject of this kind like gentlemen? Would the hon. member like to stand on his feet and make his observations now? I am willing to yield the floor.

I have listened to a fair amount of this debate and I should like to know when any hon. member suggested that the men who fought and died had, somehow, done something cowardly. I do not think anybody said that.

If you were attending as you should have been, you heard those inferences. You heard the fact that the Conservative party was charged with trying to make its members out as war heroes. If you did not hear that, you were not here. It is in Hansard; you must have read it if you have done your homework. I do mine.

Would the hon. member give the citation from Hansard to which he refers?

Canadian Flag
I do not have it at hand. I have been waiting tor over six weeks-
What about the subamendment?

I am talking now about unity-in Canada, and we must have it, yet there can be no unity as long as one party is pitted against the other on an issue like this. I am asking for a proper hearing and I am complaining that when I get up to make my contribution I am told I will be rubbed oft. Do members ot this house think for a moment that this man is capable of rubbing me off physically? He takes the protection of this house. We are not supposed to be school boys. I am not supposed to ask him out behind the shed. Thirty years ago I might have been that foolish, but we get nowhere by fighting. I am asking for unity and leadership. I have told a little story about King George VI. Would members opposite deny that this was a proper type of leadership, or that we did not have something to cling to and fight for? Are all symbols useless? If symbols mean nothing, why are we so anxious to change them? Why must we give up our Christian crosses? The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, (Mr. Douglas) a minister of the Christian gospel, said yesterday-
What page?
Read it. He said the cross of St. George was nothing more or less than a banner for rapine, murder and piracy. That is what he said as reported at page 7737.
He did not say that.

I will read it from Hansard. It is at page 7737:
St. George's cross was first used in the crusade when the kings, barons and knights of Christendom perpetrated murder, rapine and plunder in the name of Christianity-
What is inaccurate about that?

Is this really a fair summary of the use of the cross of St. George? Would one say that any country had an unblemished record in history? No. I suppose there have been British ships which fired on people without proper warning. There was the Boston tea party. There have been many crimes perpetrated throughout history. But is it fair to take one or two crimes out of history and say: This is a summary of British history? I was about to tell you, if you would keep your mouths shut for a few minutes and listen, that there are pages in Britain's history which are noble-that there are times when under

these Christian crosses Britain lived up to its responsibilities, and lived up to them alone.
There are admirers of the great United States of America, and I am one of them. But it took them a long time to hear the bugle. In the days when England fought alone, she fought under the flag I am speaking of. All I am saying is this: Is it fair to downgrade it?
I have said before, and I say again, that I am willing to accept and will accept any flag design decided upon by a fair vote in the House of Commons, if we can get together on this issue. I beg the government to do this. I beg hon. members on that side of the house to stand up and say those symbols which we have should be torn down, if that is what they believe. You are safe over there; you can threaten to rub me out, with the protection of the house behind you.
It isn't that important.
Then why did you say it?
You said it.

Hon. members opposite know who said it. But who cares, Mr. Speaker? I am not going to name them because this is beneath contempt. But I beg them not to use that kind of talk. They ask for co-operation and unity. Is it not unity we are trying to achieve? Is it not leadership? Are they not seized with the responsibility of showing leadership in their party and in their constituencies?
In this connection, Mr. Speaker, is Sir Wilfrid Laurier a reasonable reference? I think so. The Liberals were a great party in those days, and Sir Wilfrid Laurier was a statesman; he believed in the unity of Canada and he believed in that unity under the British flag. Isn't that so?
Where did he say that?

In Hansard for 1905 at page 1423, Sir Wilfrid Laurier said haste is no virtue and he begged us to approach all problems connected with Canada, her future and unity, with kindness, forbearance, love and brotherhood. He said nothing about rubbing people out. He said, "Let us get together". This was in 1905 when he was talking about bringing into the union the new provinces being created in the Northwest Territories. They did well in 1905; they created two new provinces in the Northwest Territories. I might say, Mr. Speaker, that Saskatchewan and Alberta know nothing of this division or this talk of two races fighting each other. They know where they are, but in those

provinces we have a good many other races as well; and we get along just fine because we practise what we preach.
The criticism that has come principally from the far corner of the house has been that they are the only reasonable people, the only ones who understand the problem. I warn the Liberal party to watch them. They are more clever than you think. They pretend to co-operate with you, but what do they hope to do? They hope to take over everybody in Canada who has been brainwashed with these different forms of socialism. They think the Liberals are the ones who are softened up for this sort of thing. They are getting the help of many so-called intellectuals. They have brainwashed our people. The fact that they are sincere makes no difference; the fact that they are pitifully sincere makes no difference whatsoever, because they are getting into the warp and woof of our thinking, until now it is almost sacrilege to say that socialism is not the only hope. Whom do we get this from? We get it particularly from parsons without a pulpit. I say, Mr. Speaker, that the Christian religion is the highest form of ideology that we have; it is even higher than politics. This is a standard we might all remember. That is why I mentioned King George VI. This was his standard, because he thought that to serve God was to rule, and when he did not serve God he was not fit for the throne. As far as I know, he was; and as far as I know, his daughter is.
I say to those who wish to make a republic of Canada that they would do well to remember this. Do we not need an arbitrator, a referee, in this game of politics? Do we not need an umpire in this baseball game? The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) ought to know that, because he is a baseball man. You need an umpire. Freedom wears a crown. I say to the members of the Liberal party, if you do not know anything about history, and particularly Canadian history, why not sit in this chamber and listen to the flag debate?
The fourth estate have largely abandoned their stand in this connection. They are fond of calling us Pharisees here in the pit. We also get it sometimes from some members, the defunct parsons. They are good at this sort of thing. The fourth estate include themselves, I suppose, when they say we are a bunch of hypocrites. The press love it; there is nothing they like better than talking about $18,000 a year hypocrites. But this is not true. We may have Pharisees among us, and in the press gallery there may be the odd scribe, 20220-493
Canadian Flag
in the biblical sense. There may be those who are willing to blacken white and whiten black. Let them preach to themselves. Let them write the truth up there in the press gallery.
We had a speech from the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan). To me it sounded like the bare truth. Anyway, Mr. Speaker, it went unchallenged. Was it beneath their contempt to challenge it? I think not. I admire the man who stands up and tells others the truth as he understands it. I say to hon. members opposite, have some party unity; stand behind your man and say, "This is where we stand, too". I know many of you would like to say that but you have not the courage to stand up and say, "We were not consulted". I am looking for leadership, because leadership brings unity. Without leadership we will not have unity. There are those in this house who say we have no leadership. What do you suppose they want, Mr. Speaker? They want nothing more than naked power. One of them would like to be Speaker; he wishes he had taken the job. One of them would like to be prime minister. Perhaps two or three would like to be prime minister. They say they would like to be prime minister and have the responsibility of uniting this country.
Our Prime Minister gave great hopes of this. Many of us who were here when he was chosen leader of the party had hopes of this leadership. We thought he might be another Sir Wilfrid Laurier and might take the reins and make clearcut, manly decisions and explain them to us in this house as though we were equals. The prime minister is supposed to be the first amongst equals, but that has all been changed since 1925. The Prime Minister of Canada has the sole power to dissolve parliament and appoint cabinet ministers. He has taken, in the name of a previous leader of that party, Mr. King, the supreme power in this case.
Some people tell us that what we want is good, strong leadership. This is so, Mr. Speaker; but we need good, strong leadership from a man with a conscience, a man who has courage. I want the Prime Minister to share with us this superior knowledge that he has. I represent 65,000 Canadian people, and it is my right to have questions answered in the house. I do not have my questions answered. They say to me back home, "What is the matter? Why can't you get your questions answered. What is the price of wheat going to be? What is going to be done about hog support prices?" But to this government these

Canadian Flag
are things that do not count. They say we are only farmers. Now they will not even call us farmers, because the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) is ready to call us grocery producers, manufacturers of vitamin pills. The attitude is, "We can ignore them; they are not farmers any more". We need the kind of leadership given by Sir Wilfrid Laurier. He was a great Canadian. He built Canada solidly and soundly. This is the kind of leadership we need from the prime minister of our country, whether he is a Liberal, Conservative, or whether, heaven forbid, he is a socialist, labour leader or whatever they are called. We want a prime minister who will discuss these policies with the rest of us in this house.
When I hear the hon. member for York-Humber say he was not consulted, I believe him. It has never been denied and I believe him. I believe him with all my heart. Here was a one-man truth squad. He had the courage to stand up and say: "Let the rest say what they like but I am going to tell the truth. I will put my political reputation on the line and stand the risk of being called a liar. But I am not a liar; I have told the truth". As I say, I believe him. It is this sort of man whom I would be proud to serve. One might even be tempted to join the Liberal party if there were 100 others like him. I would be proud to let him sit next to me any time, because he tells the truth, which is 90 per cent of being a good member in this house. If people cannot trust your word, then as far as I am concerned it is no use your coming here. A lie is a lie no matter how it is told. But if you tell a lie, whether it be a careless lie or any other kind of lie, at least have the moral decency to admit it. Have the courage to say that you must be wrong, or that you forgot, or that you were not in charge of the facts, and then start again. I believe in reform.
I should like to see the Liberal party as it was in the days of Laurier, when that party gave the country the leadership it needed. I do not like to see the Liberal party relying on the shaky support of the socialists, because the whole socialist philosophy is based on a false premise. They pretend that man needs no spiritual leadership. They believe that man in his own native state is some lovely co-operative creature. But I ask hon. members, what has been their experience of this in life? Is that true, or does a man need training and standards? Does he not need to stick to the rules which his father and mother taught him, to read history and to learn that the path to destruction is the path of hatred and non-

co-operation? That is the cause of all misery in the world, of all hunger and of all war. Our unemployed parsons get up and talk about the love of man. But how about honouring thy father and thy mother? How about honouring the standards of our parents?
I do not say to the French speaking people of this country that they should abandon everything they believe in. I say, stand up and be proud of them, and I will be proud of you. I am proud of the great French tradition which we have. I am proud of those who fought with us to hold off the Americans and to keep this country a free country of our own. I am proud of those men who went to western Canada in their canoes and who carved out a new country. I am proud of those who set up the two new provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta and who told the people there to try and get along together. I remember the positive things which were done, and I say we should forget this empty, petty fighting. If I am doing any empty, petty fighting I ask hon. members to challenge me by standing on their feet. They do not have to do this today; take Hansard tomorrow and read it. If they can find one word in Hansard which can be regarded as intolerance, if there is anything but gratitude for the great cooperation of the province of Quebec, tell me. I should know whether or not French Canadians are good people, because the Van Doos were in our division and I would say that they are the finest troops in the world. And in case hon. members think I am narrow about this matter, let me say that I am proud of our Governor General, Canada's greatest living soldier. I am sincerely interested in their happiness, believe me, and I hope that some day they will have the courage to stand on their feet and offer me the same co-operation and show the same respect for the traditions of my people; the same respect for my small contribution to our country's safety and present welfare. I repeat once more, whenever I speak one word against la belle province, throw it down my throat.
At the present time, Mr. Speaker, I am making a pitiful attempt to learn the French language, and I will continue to do so. I do this not as a sop to Quebec but because I admire the French language. Some of the greatest poetry and philosophy has been written in that language. I favour anything which will keep French Canadians in our country. I also favour a democratic method of getting unity, which is this: Do not hold a gun to our heads. Offer us a chance to meet you on equal ground. Let us talk it

over. Let us have a parley. There is a story of the great northwest which might help to break some of the ice here. The Idaho Kid came up to Saskatchewan. He crossed over the border and Sergeant Kelly of the mounted police was sitting in a hotel. The Idaho Kid walked up to Sergeant Kelly and said: "Are you Sergeant Kelly?". Sergeant Kelly said yes. So the Idaho Kid said: "I have always wanted to shoot a mounted policeman". Then Kelly said: "Take that .45 out of my face or I'll bite the end off it", and he stood up and arrested him.
I say you will never get anywhere if you hold any kind of gun at the head of a Canadian, whether be he French Canadian, English Canadian, Ukrainian Canadian or just a straight Canadian, which I hope we all are. Do not try to bully him, because he does not bully easily. Treat him like a gentleman. Bring him into the picture. This is the place we are supposed to discuss things and make suggestions-not give ultimatums. No ultimatum ever put on the floor of this house will be received by this party. At this point I will quote Churchill, who said never, never, never give up your principles; if you are right, stick to them. If you believe in parleys instead of the "or else" approach, if you believe in co-operation and collaboration, not force, stick to your belief. He did, and if he had not, I do not know where we would be today. That is leadership. That is the kind of leadership we want.
The Germans believed in force, although I sincerely hope that today they have changed their minds. During the last war they sent out their battleship Deutschland on the north Atlantic, and that vessel came upon a little convoy of merchant ships. The Deutschland thought it was going to have a field day. But there was a captain on board a British merchant ship who thought otherwise. He turned out of the convoy and steered straight at the Deutschland, and the Deutschland spent all her time firing on this boat so that the others were able to get away. This captain did not like the "or else" ultimatum. Then there was the battle of the river Plate. The battleship Graf Spee was discovered there by three little boats; and what happened? With co-operation, skill, guts and bravery these three little boats made her scuttle herself; she could not take it. These are events which I cannot help but admire. I am sorry, but I am not ready to throw up my traditions. I think such events as this are admired by the whole world, certainly by the free world.

I ask these hon. members for co-operation, and I say this: To have unity in Canada they must not be led down the garden path by the people who want to seize their power. The New Democratic party know they cannot beat us, but they know they can beat them because they do not know where they are going.
Oh, oh.

We know where we are going, and we are going to go there. We are going ahead toward a bigger and better united Canada, and we appeal to you people to come with us, instead of fooling around with these ideas of socialism and communism fed into you through the back door.
Oh, oh.
Look out. I appreciate the groans, because they do not think there is any danger in this at all.
What about the C.C.F.?

The C.C.F. lacked the courage to make up their minds. But their leader has his mind made up and he will take the support which would normally come to the Liberal party, being that party of the little people. Do you remember the little people, Mr. Speaker? If you are looking after the little people I suggest you consider the wages being paid to some of the people working on this hill, and rectify that situation.
Perhaps you should give some consideration to the situation in which our native people find themselves. How far have they progressed during these 97 years of progress? What do you intend to do to help them? We gave them the right to vote in an attempt to give them self-confidence, and the self-confidence of these people must be attained before they can become good citizens. You are now attempting to take away their flag. What confidence will they have in politicians, or do you think they look at all for spiritual leadership from the British crown? I may be wrong, and you can certainly find out by talking with these people, but my understanding is that they want this treaty with the Queen to last for as long as the sun shines and the waters run. I do not think they will approve of politicians who attempt to change that treaty. What are you going to do after you remove that which is the Queen's flag in the eyes of these people?
Can you honestly suggest that you desire to retain our overseas associations; and if you do not, why are you not honest and say so? If you desire to form a republican party

Canadian Flag
I am sure some citizens in Canada will support you. If you agree with that idea you should have the courage to stand up for it. We are now experiencing an evolutionary state and indicating our belief in the advancement of political science. Where do you honestly stand in this regard?
I stand behind British tradition under the British crown. Everyone is aware that the British crown has no physical force, that it is a rubber stamp for our government; but there is a principle of fair play and justice involved. Governments quail before these standards if they are well informed, and I suggest that we take a serious look at our problems. We should seriously consider our present symbols of tradition.
I am sure some members at least on this side of the house honour the fatherland of their parents in the same way I expect hon. members opposite honour their parents' fatherland. I have never pretended that there are not basically two origins of Canadian people, and I respect both.
Perhaps if we could turn back the pages of time and start again, a completely new flag would be acceptable. I can envisage one suggestion that might be acceptable if we could go back in time. Perhaps the union jack quartered with the lily banner of France, following the lines of heraldry, would be acceptable as representing racial origin. I do not think we can go back in time and forget tradition. Certainly there is no indication of that in the tenor of this debate to date.
When members on this side of the house speak on this flag issue they do not receive the kind of encouragement I would expect from individuals who are attempting to take part in the debate in a spirit of conciliation. I agree with the principle of equal rights, but one question in this regard has never been answered: Why must we desert that which we believe in; why should there be a oneway deal?
I do not see anything in those traditions I revere which is divisive. I would be the first individual in this house to suggest that Canada is a great sovereign nation, because we are in fact a sovereign nation. The Queen does nothing more than place a legal stamp of approval on that which we wish to do. Whatever we propose she accepts. What more can we ask? We certainly need a referee to rule in respect of problems between our two originating peoples, who have not yet reached a mutual understanding in the way that Laurier envisaged. Sir Wilfrid Laurier admitted, as I think we must, that there are

troubles and difficulties between our peoples. If we continue to pretend, as do our socialist friends, that we are loving brothers together, I do not think we will find a way out of our difficulty. The socialists believe that all we have to do to settle the difficulties is dissolve the two old parties. They think everyone would then be happy. I am surprised that the members on the other side of the house are not aware of that fact. Time and time again members of the small parties to my left have castigated our leaders.
I hope you will forgive me for not knowing all the well known quotations of Woods-worth, but he said in the 1930's that the Liberals say terrible things about the Conservatives, the Conservatives say terrible things about the Liberals, and we socialists agree with both sides, that neither of them is any good. Lo and behold, some of the intellectualists in this country have taken up that hue and cry. That cry has been taken up as well by certain members of the press and has become Canada's national amusement, second only to Beatlemania. We criticize your leader in exactly the same terms you use to criticize our leader. I suggest as a warning that we are playing into the hands of those little groups down to my left in the corner who wish to seize power.
Our parliamentary system was set up on the premise that we are all gentlemen and would attempt to settle our disagreements by consultation and negotiation. I suggest that when we rise in our places to curse each other we are playing into the hands of those small groups. If we play the parliamentary game properly, and I use that term in its proper sense, we would have little difficulty solving our problems.
I think there should be a general reformation so that some members of this house have liberal feelings, while others approach things conservatively. The Liberals now suggest that we make haste hastily, while the historic approach of the Conservative party has been, let us make haste slowly. Sir Wilfrid Laurier said, let us be careful, because haste in itself is not good. I should like to know why there is a need for haste today in respect of this flag issue. Why must we settle the issue now in view of our past 97 years of existence without a distinctive flag? We have used the British crown as a symbol of tradition. I am not suggesting that it is universally popular or acceptable. Very few people refer to the British crown tradition as a basis of argument. Certainly that argument is not possible

when we use it, and I imagine less popular when you use it.

speechtext: Order. I must advise the hon. gentleman that his time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, in taking part today in this debate I should like to make reference to certain statements made in recent days, and call attention particularly to the remarks of the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), as they appear at page 7643 of Hansard. That hon. member indicated his sincere belief that the government had made some concessions in respect of a free vote. He has apparently been taken in. I did not realize he was the gullible type. The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) has hoodwinked him by suggesting there would be a free vote and that there would not be an election as a result of the outcome of that vote.
Mr. Speaker, I should like also to refer to the acceptance of the free vote suggestion by the leader of the New Democratic party. His remarks are recorded at page 7739 of Hansard. That hon. gentleman said:
I readily acknowledge to the Prime Minister that the government has made the major concessions, and almost the only concessions that have been made on this issue. The government has agreed to a free vote, so that an election is not hanging on the outcome.
Those two gentlemen are men of considerable experience in this house, and I should have thought they would be able to interpret the offer made by the Prime Minister with greater acumen. I ask them to qualify their belief in respect of that offer after considering the attitude taken by members on both sides of this house. In support of my feeling in this regard I refer to the whip of the Liberal party, who has concerned himself greatly with pairs. He is concerned about the absence from the house possibly for very good reasons, of members of his own party, and has put forth great efforts to cover them with pairs from this side of the house, whether from the Conservative party or some other group in the house. If the leader of the New Democratic party and the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) really believe that such a thing as a free vote will take place on this matter, why then does the Liberal whip concern himself with pairs? It is very obvious that in a vote considered to be free the necessity for pairs goes out the window. So the idea of a free vote promoted by the Prime Minister has been denied by his own party whip in seeking pairi, and I
Canadian Flag
would hope that the leader of the N.D.P. and the hon. member for Port Arthur would be able to see the situation before us now more clearly.
As found on page 7739 of Hansard, the leader of the New Democratic party made something else quite clear in his speech. My interpretation of his remarks indicates to me, and I am quite sure would indicate to all members of the house upon examination, that the members of that party, since he is speaking for them as their leader, are obviously against the new flag that has been presented to the house. As I understand the situation, they have prepared an amendment embodying a flag that they think will unite Canada. However, I should like to read into the record one very worthwhile contribution that the leader of that party made to the debate yesterday in order to substantiate my argument at this time. As found on the page to which I have referred, he said:
I think we have to begin by remembering that dealing with a flag issue is not the same as dealing with a legislative matter. If this was a matter of some important legislative significance, there are parliamentary means of bringing the matter to a decision. In respect of this question, even if we could force a decision it would be a Pyrrhic decision. A flag adopted by Canada should represent the consensus and should be launched with the general support of the vast majority of the Canadian people. It should be an instrument for forging unity rather than creating division, and no flag will accomplish that if it is conceived in controversy and born in bitterness.
I heartily endorse this statement of the leader of the New Democratic party and I call the attention of the house to the fact that any further pushing on the part of the government to try to put their flag across is a definite contradiction of these remarks which were referred to yesterday by the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Dupuis) as a very good contribution to the debate. The minister can check his own words. He said he was in full support of what the leader of the New Democratic party had said. Therefore he must be in full support of the idea that for the government to push this matter any further is ridiculous because bitterness is certainly evident and has been evident in the last few days.
I should also like to refer to remarks made by the Prime Minister following the vote yesterday. As found on page 7736 of Hansard, he said:
Mr. Speaker, I can understand the right hon. gentleman's feeling of frustration, when only 44 members of his party were here: but I am at a loss to understand his irritation at being delayed from attending what he himself used to refer to

Canadian Flag
ironically as an egghead conference. As a result, Mr. Speaker, I would ask you to give a ruling whether there is any question of privilege whatever involved in the point the right hon. gentleman has raised.
My objection to these remarks of the Prime Minister is that they are unfair, uncalled for and false. The Prime Minister said that only 44 members of this party were here, and again I come back to the Liberal whip's efforts to find pairs for members of his party. I would also point out that having only 85 members of his party here or, to use the words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp), 85 members of the group he is leading, does not constitute an attendance record about which he should brag. The Prime Minister's words were uncalled for, unfair and false. There were more than 44 Conservative members here. A considerable number of Conservatives did not vote for the simple reason that they were covering members of the Liberal party who were absent. This is an arrangement made among members. I personally had made such an arrangement. At no time did I rise and announce I was paired with such and such a member because I consider this to be a useless waste of the time of the house. If I am going to co-operate with a member I will pair with him. This is a matter between the two of us and something which we will look after ourselves. The Prime Minister's reference that there were only 44 members of this party present was not in accordance with the facts. I might also say that while I have recognized a pair during the votes that have taken place in the last week or so I have made it quite clear to the member with whom I have had this arrangement that when the house does have the opportunity to vote on the flag resolution itself I have no intention of doing anything other than to vote against it.
I should also like to refer to some other remarks made during the debate and with your indulgence, Mr. Speaker, I might also refer to certain rulings that have been made. On page 7540 of Hansard we find this remark by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill):
No one can say I did not listen intently, or with courtesy and politeness, to the right hon. gentleman when he was speaking, as did my hon. friends, and I think I might be permitted to say what X have to say without these noisy interruptions.
He went on to give the house a dressing down because he considered he was being interrupted. I might also say that when I attempted to ask a question that evening the Chair ruled that fair play should be involved in the carrying on of the debate. I took it
[Mr. Maclnnis.l
from that remark that any attempt by me to ask a question of the member speaking at the time was being very unfair. I refer again to the fact that the Speaker himself said that no one had interrupted the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) and I call attention again to these words of the Minister of Transport:
No one can say X did not listen intently, or with courtesy and politeness-
In that regard I would refer to the speech made by the Leader of the Opposition where you will find that he was interrupted on 40 occasions, 9 of the interruptions being by the Minister of Transport. I am sorry he is not in his place. He maintains he is the most courteous gentleman in the house but he has the rudest manner of any member of the house. He maintained that he listened with courtesy when the fact is that if hon. members will check the speech of the Leader of the Opposition they will find that that very minister interrupted nine times.
I would also refer to page 7539 of Hansard where certain remarks made by the Minister of Transport are found, which I maintained at that time were in direct contradiction of the contribution made by the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan). Before the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) leaves the house I should like to thank her for the kind invitation she extended to me a few moments ago. I know this is not in keeping with the tenor of my other remarks but I do wish to express my appreciation to her for the invitation.
To get back to the remarks made by the Minister of Transport, which I say were in direct contradiction to those made by the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan), I might point out that he maintained the Prime Minister made statements on "The Nation's Business" in respect to a distinctive Canadian flag, and I might also point out that in the second last full paragraph on page 7539 he said this:
When the present Prime Minister said this in 1960, it was accepted, and that position was accepted by the Liberal party, and it was the position we took at the election of 1962. It was in our literature.
Herein lies a direct contradiction, and it is very interesting to point out that each time there seems to be a difference of opinion on the Conservative side of the house the Liberals, in their ability to put across lies and propaganda, will point the finger and say, "Ah, ah, division; another follower leaving your leader." I would call to your attention the remark made by the hon. member for

Cochrane (Mr. Habel) this afternoon, when there was a difference of opinion expressed by him with respect to the hon. member for York-Humber. Did he refer to him as a deserter of the party policy, or as deserting the ranks? No. In his opinion he was a black sheep. This is how the Liberal party refers to somebody who does not fall in line with the dictates of their leader.

On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is right when he says I referred to a black sheep. What I said was that in a group there was always a black sheep, but I added that it was the hon. member's privilege to stand by his convictions. That is what I said, and I do not want the hon. member to change my words.
On a question of privilege, I would like to ask the hon. member for Cochrane if he is aware this is a free vote?
A free vote, in my opinion, is one where the hon. member has a right to vote in the same way as hon. members opposite will have the right to vote.
The hon. member for Cochrane has explained his position, and I think the hon. member for Cape Breton South should now proceed with the rest of his remarks.
Mr. Speaker, I would like your ruling on whether or not the term black sheep is parliamentary?
For the benefit of the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Nasserden) I personally do not consider it an unparliamentary term, and I so rule.

I did not quite catch your ruling, Mr. Speaker.
The Acting Speaker (Mr. Cameron (High
Park)): I said I did not consider the reference to a black sheep was an unparliamentary term.

Mr. Speaker, I am in full agreement with that; I was taking no exception to the use of the phrase. I might also say that if the hon. member for Cochrane had a question of privilege, we all realize each and every one of us are here as individuals and we will vote according to our conscience, provided our party dictates will permit; and I point out that very recently with respect to the legislation put forward providing for the trustees I saw fit to go my own way. I am sure all members willingly would do the same, and if such were the case the outcome
Canadian Flag
of a vote on the flag, provided it were a free vote, would be anything other than what the Liberal party is planning today.
On another question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I do not think the hon. member has a right to question our consciences. We will certainly vote according to our consciences.
Mr. Speaker, I never-

Order. I was under the impression we were debating an amendment dealing with how the results of a plebiscite, if it were held, should be divulged. It seems to me the hon. member for Cape Breton South is straying a fairly considerable distance from that particular subject. I think the hon. member for Cochrane has a point and that there should be no reflection or imputation as to how hon. members express their opinions in regard to the matter before the house. I am speaking to the hon. member for Cape Breton South in a kindly spirit. I hope he will take it that way and will refrain from making remarks which I feel are entirely uncalled for.

Mr. Speaker, I accept your ruling. I at no time tried to question the conscience of the hon. member for Cochrane. I would only remind him that possibly he should question his own. The ruling in reference to the subamendment is quite accurate. However, I would remind each and every member of the house that if I am going to be curtailed to speak on the subamendment only, I would suggest to the house that possibly starting with the speech made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp), and winding up as late as last evening with the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Dupuis)-
I talked about the referendum all the time.

Mr. Speaker, on this matter I would ask the Minister without Portfolio to examine his speech and he will find it was practically all made up of quotations referring to the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Horner).
About the referendum.

He was quoting continually from speeches made in 1960 or 1961, prior to the flag resolution, or whatever year he chose to look up. Before the hon. member for Cochrane imagined he had a question of privilege I was pointing out that there were

Canadian Flag
several contradictions made here in the house. We have heard a good, detailed explanation by the hon. member for York-Humber as to what was the stand of the Liberal party prior to the last election in reference to a distinctive Canadian flag. This was detailed and backed up by illustrations from pamphlets which he had. I might also say here that the riflings coming from the Chair seem to be awkward to understand in that the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) came into the house and he had with him a brochure dealing with different flags, and the ruling was that he was not allowed to have any such thing in the house. But the Minister without Portfolio on occasion has had what he called an authentic example of the three maple leaves on one stem, and of course he has had his bumper stickers to display. At no time did the Chair rule that the hon. member should not have these in on display, while at the same time ruling that the hon. member for Edmonton West should not have with him a pamphlet showing different flags of different nationalities.
When the hon. member for York-Humber was putting forward his argument he did it with detail and with pamphlets to support his argument. Then the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) took exception. Now, Mr. Speaker, it is quite obvious someone is lying. Of course it is for us to decide, for each and every one of us to decide who was lying. All I can say is that when I am confronted with the written evidence by one member, the hon. member for York-Humber, I therefore have to accept his side of the story. The Minister of Transport was not telling the truth when he said this was carried in their campaign literature. At least he did not in any way support his argument, as did the hon. member for York-Humber. So we can understand from the arguments put forward that the Minister of Transport, representing Bona-vista-Twillingate, was entirely wrong in the -if I may use the term-accusation which was pointed towards the hon. member for York-Humber, which was done also this afternoon by the hon. member from Scarborough, and I might also say the yapper from Kootenay East who is no longer in his seat, who very seldom makes a contribution from his feet. He is probably now somewhere about the city saying what he said in the House of Commons, but he never gets on his feet and makes a contribution. He likes to sit there interjecting day after day after day, and when he is on his feet he is only reading

something passed to him from the minister's office in order to bring certain information before the house.
As I said, the hon. member for York-Humber substantiated every argument he put forward, and at no time to my knowledge did the Liberal party put before the people of Canada anything in the way of a definite decision to bring forward a distinctive Canadian flag.
Speaking of distinctive Canadian flags, the Minister without Portfolio is here. I would very much like to find out how he can qualify a statement he made last night, and how another hon. member, I think from York North, can qualify a statement he made some time ago in this debate, and how other members of the Liberal party can substantiate their arguments in respect to a distinctive Canadian flag. Should the Minister without Portfolio be wondering just what he did say last night, I call his attention to page 7762 of Hansard where he will find these words recorded in the second column:
What about the second flag?
You should begin by settling the first problem. You are so mixed up with the first -we will speak about the second later.
That is right.

The Minister without Portfolio and the hon. member for Cochrane say: "That is right". Fine. They are proposing a distinctive Canadian flag, they say. But a distinctive Canadian flag can be distinctive only as one flag; it cannot be distinctive as two. The minister is prepared to get up and talk about a second flag, and the hon. member for Cochrane says "That is right".
Does the hon. member wish me to answer?
Is the hon. member yielding the floor to the Minister without Portfolio?
It is apparent that I am not. I am still on my feet.
If the hon. member does not want to have an answer he should not ask questions.

I did not ask a question. I might possibly be prepared to yield the floor to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays). He seems to have something to say, though he says very little about agriculture. If he has something to say about the flag I would consider yielding to him for a few moments. It would only take a few moments

for him to get his views across, if he does not know any more about the flag than he does about agriculture.
Members opposite talk about a distinctive flag. But how can anybody qualify that idea by talking about a second flag? I am sorry to see the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) about to leave, because I had a question I wished to put to him. With regard to the opening remarks made on this subject by the hon. member for York North (Mr. Addison)-I do not have the words before me, but they can be checked and if anyone wishes to raise a question of privilege he can do so-I should like to repeat much the same comment. The hon. member said when he spoke on this subject, in his introductory remarks: "The first flag I intend to speak about-". Then there is a second flag. What is distinctive about proposing that there should be two flags?
How did this situation come about? Again I am sorry the Minister of Transport is not here. It is well known that the premier of Newfoundland insisted that the union jack should be included and that it should be written into the bill. Well, there was some cloak and dagger work going on in the background, and I repeat that I think the Minister of Transport had a direct hand in preparing this legislation. I think it took him about two weeks to do it, but finally he came up with the idea that there should be a two flag resolution. Again I ask the question: What can be distinctive about something which is put forward in two parts? Nothing can be distinctive as long as it is brought before the house in a two-part resolution. The second part, in my opinion, is a dubious method of trying to put it across to the premier of Newfoundland that his wishes are being met. They are not being met and the premier stands a good chance of being the victim of a complete double cross down the line.
I hope the hon. member whom I see resuming his seat is not doing so with the intention of telling the house that he hopes to support the maple leaf flag as being one distinctive flag.
I should like to remind the hon. member that I have already spoken on this subject, so he might refer to Hansard if he wishes to know my views.

If the hon. member is so keen on putting forward the idea of a three maple leaf flag I suggest he should not overlook the opportunity of speaking a second time. It will take him a lot more speeches 20220-494
Canadian Flag
before he can convince Mr. Smallwood in Newfoundland that he is getting what he asked for. He did not get the union jack written into the legislation as he wanted, but the Minister of Transport, with some help from other quarters, put forward this dubious method of a two part resolution as a means of satisfying him.
I should like to hear from the members representing the maritime provinces. I should like to hear the members from Halifax, Anti-gonish and Yarmouth stand in their places and give unqualified support to this three maple leaf design. What the Halifax members have done so far is to offer only qualified support, after they had been given prior information with respect to what the resolution would contain. Then they made statements which were, in effect, statements of qualified support for the resolution favouring the three maple leaf flag. Let them speak. After all, they have been invited by their own leader to do so. The Prime Minister wants every member to make a contribution. I ask them now to get up and express unqualified support for this three maple leaf flag. How many of them intend to do so. The hon. member for Cochrane spoke about examining one's conscience. Let them examine their consciences and see whether they can give the Prime Minister's maple leaf design the unqualified support he is trying to infer he has received. The hon. member for York-Humber made it clear that there was division in the Liberal party. I, too, made it clear when I challenged members of the government to get up and say that they, too, gave the Prime Minister's design their unqualified support. The flag proposed by the Prime Minister does not have the unqualified support of his backbenchers. It does not even have the unqualified support of his cabinet ministers.
Does the hon. member want me to answer him? He was asking me to stand up and answer him. If he wants an answer, let me give it.
I would very much like-

The hon. member for Cape Breton South has challenged a number of members of the house to get up and make statements and I think he should probably be prepared to permit them to do so, having made that challenge.

I hope to be permitted to finish the remarks I was making with respect to this question. I said I challenged any

Canadian Flag
cabinet minister to get up in the house and make a statement of unqualified approval for the proposed new flag. And when we come to the minister whose views were made known directly to me, I will confront him with his remarks and back my statements with witnesses who were present when he made his views known about his feelings with regard to the three maple leaf flag.
Name him.

I do not have to name him. He is perfectly capable of coming into the house and speaking for himself. Let this cabinet minister explain his position to the Prime Minister and to the house. To use the dignified expression of the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Tardif), let him have the intestinal fortitude to stand up and tell the house and the Prime Minister what he told me in the presence of witnesses, namely that he does not understand the choice of the three maple leaf design and that he is also-
Name him.
Why should I?
Because we should like to know whom you are talking about.

The Minister without Portfolio wishes to find out who in his party or in his cabinet does not favour the three maple leaf flag. I suggest he should keep his ears open. It has been made quite evident to me and other members of this party that many members on the other side of the house have found themselves in a very embarrassing position, because they freely admit that correspondence they have received from their constituents proves to them without a doubt that the three maple leaf flag does not have the support of their constituents; and with regard to those members to whom I am referring, in most cases their constituents are standing firm on behalf of the red ensign. Why are not these members coming forward and making themselves heard? Why should not the members of the Liberal party stand up, at the invitation of the Prime Minister, and make quite clear to the people of this country and the members of this house just why they support the three maple leaf flag?
Then let us have a vote.

Will the hon. member for Cochrane stop his yapping? I have had experience with the hon. member previously, right up in his own constituency. My experience was in sitting down as a guest in his constituency, with a vacant chair that was

left for him, and he did not show up. I have been in his riding, Mr. Speaker, and I might say that the reception I got was one the hon. member should have been there to get for himself.
They did not elect a new member, though.

Why should not these members stand up and give their reasons for supporting the three maple leaf flag? They have been invited by the Prime Minister to do so. Why should they not rise and give his design their unqualified support? I should like to hear from the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer). I should like to hear from the Prime Minister himself. I wonder why these hon. gentlemen permit their speeches to go out in a brochure that is spread across this country and foreign countries, because in those speeches the red ensign is designated as a distinctive Canadian flag. Speeches appear in this brochure by the Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) and the Minister of National Defence. Part of that brochure contains a card displaying the red ensign as a distinctive Canadian flag. Am I to understand that the Minister of National Defence, the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Prime Minister are going to withdraw their speeches from that particular brochure?
The Minister without Portfolio wants people named; he wants this, he wants that. He spent 50 minutes speaking on this subject last night. I agree that there were many interjections and interruptions, but that is usual here.
There were 11 interruptions from you.
Seven?
Eleven.
Then I did very well. In view of what the Minister without Portfolio was saying, he deserved 70 interruptions, not seven.
Eleven.

I might say, Mr. Speaker, that if the Minister without Portfolio does not stop embarrassing his own government he might not be a minister, even one without portfolio. He spoke on this subject last night for 50 minutes. I agree with him that there were many interruptions. I believe that my interruptions mainly consisted of points of order, and on one occasion I referred to a

ruling the Chair made and I was quickly corrected. Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, one of the points of order I wanted to raise was this. I was reminded last night by the Chair that the rules do cover this question, and nobody is allowed to refer to votes. But the surprising thing is that when the ruling was put into effect last night it only followed by a few hours the Prime Minister's reference to a vote that had taken place. Nobody saw fit to rise and point out to the Prime Minister that he was breaking the rules. However, the minute somebody on this side of the house did this, it was immediately said it was against the rules. Many rules have been broken on the other side of the house. I say to the Minister without Portfolio that although he spoke for 50 minutes on this subject last night, not one word did he say in support of the three maple leaf flag, the flag of his Prime Minister. It is true that he accepted the Prime Minister's invitation to speak on this matter, but he did not put forward anything in support of the three maple leaf flag- not one word. As was mentioned in the house last night, the chief huckster of the Liberal party in this particular matter has not had one word to say in support of this flag. Having had 50 minutes in which to promote his own little enterprise, I am surprised that he did not see fit to deal with this question. Possibly there was no profit motive to move him.
You are talking about the sticker-licker.
That is exactly right. He sells bumper stickers, as I understand it. There was no profit motive-
There should be one on your mouth.
As I understand it, Mr. Speaker, the Minister without Portfolio is selling bumper stickers at a price-
Do you want one for your mouth?
Order.

Will you speak a little louder, Mr. Speaker, the minister cannot hear you. It is very odd, Mr. Speaker, that when there are interjections from this side of the house, the Chair is quite anxious to rise immediately at times and call us to order, as
Business of the House happened in the case of the Minister of Transport. I see that minister has arrived in the chamber, that man who tries to promote himself as the most polite and gracious member of the house. That is what he claims. He says, "I listened without interrupting". He says he is very gracious, and so on; but since he is here I would remind him that the last time he rose in the house and tried to promote himself as the Emily Post of parliament-
Oh, oh.

-if he would look back just a few pages of Hansard prior to making that statement he would find out how mannerly he is. He is most rude. What he said in his own defence can be contradicted if one refers to Hansard a few pages earlier, where it will be seen that he interrupted the Leader of the Opposition on nine occasions, although he claimed he did not interrupt him at all.
I now return to the subject of the Minister without Portfolio. There was no profit motive involved, so during those 50 minutes he did not say a word in defence of the three maple leaf flag. Yet he sells bumper stickers, I understand, at a higher price than one would pay elsewhere. Therefore the profit motive moves the Minister without Portfolio. I would say, Mr. Speaker, that this profit motive might easily rule him out of the position he now enjoys as Minister without Portfolio.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock?
You said nothing intelligent in your speech.
Mr. Speaker, assuming that we go on with this debate tomorrow, may I ask the house leader what he intends to call for Friday in the way of estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with the assumption alluded to by the hon. member, on Friday we would begin by a discussion of the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare, after which we would deal with the estimates of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. Then if there is time left we will discuss the estimates of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration.

At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
